A votive church on the island of Giudecca in Venice, facing the city across the Giudecca Canal. The Senate vowed it in thanks for the end of the plague that killed some 46,000 Venetians, a quarter or more of the city, in 1575 and 1576, and gave the design to Andrea Palladio. The patriarch laid the first stone on 3 May 1577 and the church was consecrated in 1592, after Palladio's death. At the wish of Pope Gregory XIII it was given to the Capuchin friars, who still live beside it.

The Senate wanted a square plan, but Palladio made a long single nave with three chapels on each side, leading to a domed crossing, as a pilgrimage church needed. The white front, raised on a wide base with fifteen steps up to the door, draws on the Pantheon in Rome: a tall temple front laid over a wider, lower one. A statue of the Redeemer stands on the dome. Inside, one Corinthian order runs around all the walls, and the paintings include works by Veronese, the Bassano family and Tintoretto's workshop.

Each year the doge and the senators crossed to the church from the Zattere on a bridge of boats to hear Mass. The Festa del Redentore keeps the custom on the third Sunday of July, with fireworks the night before and a procession over a pontoon bridge. With Santa Maria della Salute, built after the plague of 1630, it is one of the city's plague churches.
